questions.question: Your nightly Spring Batch job that used to finish in 2 hours is now taking 6 hours and occasionally failing. How do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.title: Scenario — Slow and Failing Batch Job, Production Debug Walkthrough
questions.direct_answer: **Frame it as a triage** — treat slowdown and failure as potentially separate problems. Gather data first: **`StepExecution` history** (start/end, read/write/skip counts, exceptions), **DB-side metrics** (query plans, lock waits, replication lag), **host metrics** (CPU, GC), and **data-volume trends**. Compare a recent slow run against an older fast run to identify what changed. Typical culprits in order of likelihood: **data growth**, **index regression**, **lock contention**, **chunk size or JDBC batching misconfigured**, **retry storms**, and **resource contention**. Fix in tiers: optimize query and add index → increase chunk size and JDBC batching → introduce partitioning → move to off-peak window. Always document the diagnosis so it isn't rediscovered next quarter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Production debugging mindset, familiarity with Batch execution metadata, DB/infra troubleshooting, progressive tuning
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Jumping to 'add more threads' without identifying the real bottleneck
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss `/actuator`, Micrometer, tailing `execution_context` for reader progress, correlating Batch metrics with DB slow-query logs and deploy markers

sections.title: Frame It as a Triage Before Touching Knobs
sections.content:
A batch job that **slowed from 2h to 6h** and **occasionally fails** has three possible states. Separating them is essential because the remedies differ.

**Three states to distinguish:**
- **Throughput regression** — each chunk takes longer than before
- **Volume growth** — rows/sec stable but the dataset grew
- **Failure-driven slowdown** — retries and rollbacks inflate total time

**Triage discipline:**
- Don't tune what you haven't measured
- Capture data → form hypothesis → test fix → verify → document
- Treat the batch job as a production system with SLAs, dashboards, and runbooks

**Typical root-cause distribution from real production incidents:**
- ~40% unplanned data growth
- ~25% DB query regression (new code, stale stats, index drift)
- ~15% external service slowness triggering retry storms
- ~10% infrastructure change (VPC, storage tier, DB sizing)
- ~10% other (library upgrade, config drift)

The **first question to ask** is 'how big was last month's dataset versus this month?' — answers the problem in five minutes more often than you'd expect.

sections.title: Diagnostic Flow for a Slow and Failing Batch Job
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    alert["Alert: 6h run with occasional failures"]
    alert --> gather["Gather data"]
    gather --> stepExec["StepExecution history (counts, timings, skip, rollback)"]
    gather --> dbMetrics["DB metrics (slow query log, lock waits, replication lag)"]
    gather --> hostMetrics["Host metrics (CPU, GC, IO)"]
    gather --> growth["Data volume trend (rows over time)"]
    stepExec --> compare{"Compare slow run vs fast run"}
    dbMetrics --> compare
    hostMetrics --> compare
    growth --> compare
    compare --> hyp1["Hypothesis A: throughput regression (query, index, lock)"]
    compare --> hyp2["Hypothesis B: volume growth (rows grew)"]
    compare --> hyp3["Hypothesis C: failure-driven (retry storms, rollbacks)"]
    hyp1 --> fix1["Fix: query plan, index, writer tuning"]
    hyp2 --> fix2["Fix: partitioning, async, larger chunk"]
    hyp3 --> fix3["Fix: address upstream, tune skip and retry"]
    fix1 --> verify["Re-run and compare metrics"]
    fix2 --> verify
    fix3 --> verify
    verify --> doc["Document runbook and add alerts"]
```

sections.title: Phase 1 — Immediate Data Gathering (15 Minutes)
sections.content:
The Batch metadata in `BATCH_*` tables is your best friend. Pull it first.

**StepExecution history**

```sql
SELECT je.job_execution_id, je.start_time, je.end_time,
       EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (je.end_time - je.start_time)) / 60 AS duration_min,
       je.status, je.exit_code
FROM batch_job_execution je
WHERE je.job_instance_id IN (
    SELECT job_instance_id FROM batch_job_instance WHERE job_name = 'nightly_etl'
)
ORDER BY je.start_time DESC LIMIT 20;

SELECT step_name, start_time, end_time,
       read_count, write_count, filter_count,
       read_skip_count, write_skip_count, rollback_count, commit_count,
       EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (end_time - start_time)) AS duration_sec
FROM batch_step_execution
WHERE job_execution_id = :id
ORDER BY start_time;
```

**Look for:**
- Which step grew most? Concentrates blame
- `rollback_count` climbing — retries firing on each rollback
- `write_skip_count` increasing — skip listener data shows which records
- `read_count` vs last month — volume growth

**Actuator endpoints (if exposed)**
- `GET /actuator/metrics/spring.batch.job` — Micrometer timers
- `GET /actuator/metrics/spring.batch.chunk.write` — per-chunk write latency
- `GET /actuator/metrics/spring.batch.item.process` — processor latency
- Compare p50/p99 across runs; spike in p99 = intermittent slowness

**DB-side metrics**
- Slow query log during the window
- `pg_stat_statements` (Postgres) / Performance Schema (MySQL) for top-time queries
- Lock waits and blocked sessions: `pg_stat_activity`, `SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS`
- Replication lag if reading from a replica

**Host metrics**
- CPU saturation (>80% sustained)
- GC pauses (`jstat -gc <pid>` or `gc.log`)
- Heap growth — possible memory leak from over-caching skipped records
- Disk IO on the DB host (IOPS or bandwidth exhaustion)

**Compare two runs**
- Pick a recent 6h run and an older 2h run
- Diff step-level metrics; the step that grew most is the bottleneck

This phase usually points at one of the three categories: volume growth, throughput regression, or failure-driven slowdown.

sections.title: Phase 2 — Hypothesis Testing by Category
sections.content:
Once data is in hand, test the dominant hypothesis first. Most incidents fall into one of these four categories.

**A. Volume growth — most common, easiest to spot**
- `read_count` 2-3x larger than last month → dataset grew; throughput unchanged
- Fixes:
  - **Partitioning** — split work by range/hash; run workers in parallel (3-10× speedup)
  - **Incremental load** — only process new/changed rows using a watermark column
  - **Archival** — move old data to cold storage so working set stays bounded
  - **Off-peak scheduling** — earlier window, less infra contention

**B. Throughput regression — same volume, slower**
- Reader query: `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`
  - Missing or stale index on a new WHERE/JOIN column
  - Statistics out of date — run `ANALYZE`
  - Plan changed to nested-loop over a now-large table; force hash join if needed
- Writer slower:
  - JDBC batching enabled? `spring.jdbc.batch.size=100` for JDBC writer; for JPA `hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50` and `hibernate.order_inserts=true`
  - Too many indexes on target — drop-during-load + recreate for bulk
  - Triggers / CDC adding per-row overhead
- Locks:
  - Concurrent job writing same table → serialize or partition by key
  - Long reader transaction holding shared locks → switch to pagination + short transactions

**C. Failure-driven slowdown — retries or rollbacks**
- `rollback_count` climbing = retries firing; each retry re-runs the chunk
- Identify cause:
  - Which exception is being retried? `BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION_EXCEPTION` detail table
  - Truly transient? If `ConnectException` hits a service that's consistently slow, retrying makes it worse
- Fixes:
  - Make processor **idempotent** so retries are safe
  - Tune `retryLimit` down if retries rarely succeed
  - Add **circuit breaker** around external calls
  - Move to **async processor** so failures don't block the whole chunk
  - For persistent failure, **fail fast** and surface the error for humans

**D. Infrastructure regressions**
- DB host downsized after a cost-cutting exercise
- Switched to a slower storage tier (lower IOPS)
- JVM upgrade introduced GC regression — try G1 → ZGC for low pauses
- Network latency between app and DB increased (new VPC, firewall inspection)

**Quick-win tuning checklist (before architectural changes)**
- Chunk size: try 100 → 500 → 1000 → 2000; measure each
- JDBC batch size: align with chunk size
- Add missing index on reader query
- Run `ANALYZE` (Postgres) / let MySQL auto-analyze
- Disable non-essential triggers/constraints for load; re-enable + validate after
- Move execution to off-peak window

If none of these recover the 4-hour gap, move to scaling strategies.

sections.title: Phase 3 — Scaling and Long-Term Fixes
sections.content:
When tuning isn't enough, pick a scaling strategy that fits the workload.

**1. Partition the heavy step (biggest lever)**
- Hash by a natural key (`customer_id`, `region_id`) for uniform distribution
- Grid size = number of cores across worker fleet
- Each worker gets its own DB connection — watch the pool size
- Realistic gain: 3-10× depending on DB throughput and worker count

**2. Async processor/writer**
- Per-item external calls (e.g., address validation API per item)
- `AsyncItemProcessor` with thread pool 20-50
- Writer unwraps `Future<T>`
- Gain: 10-100× for high-latency calls

**3. Read from replica, write to primary**
- Reader query on read replica avoids contending with write workload
- Watch replication lag — just-written data may not be on the replica

**4. Bulk-load bypasses**
- Postgres `COPY FROM` via `CopyManager` — 10-100× faster than row-by-row insert
- MySQL `LOAD DATA INFILE`
- Sometimes a tasklet invoking a bulk loader beats a Batch writer

```java
@Bean
public Step bulkLoadStep(JobRepository repo, PlatformTransactionManager tx,
                         DataSource ds) {
    return new StepBuilder("bulkLoad", repo)
            .tasklet((contribution, ctx) -> {
                try (Connection conn = ds.getConnection()) {
                    PgConnection pg = conn.unwrap(PgConnection.class);
                    CopyManager copy = pg.getCopyAPI();
                    try (FileReader reader = new FileReader("/staging/orders.csv")) {
                        long rows = copy.copyIn(
                            "COPY orders(id, customer_id, amount) FROM STDIN CSV",
                            reader);
                        log.info("Bulk loaded {} rows", rows);
                    }
                }
                return RepeatStatus.FINISHED;
            }, tx)
            .build();
}
```

**5. Change strategy entirely**
- Stream instead of batch: CDC (Debezium) + Kafka + downstream consumers — always up-to-date, no nightly run
- Near-real-time materialized views (Postgres `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY`)
- Purpose-built analytical engines (Redshift, BigQuery) for reporting

**Validation and verification**
- Re-run on non-prod with prod-like data volumes
- Measure: total duration, p99 per-chunk duration, skip/rollback counts, DB load
- A/B test old vs new configuration before full rollout
- Prepare rollback plan: revert config + re-run failed window

**Documentation and runbook update**
- Add a 'slow job' diagnostic runbook with exact SQL queries, actuator endpoints, log commands
- Record root cause and fix in incident log
- Add alerts: duration > 3h (warning), > 5h (page), skip rate > 1%, rollback count > 10
- Add dashboard: duration trend, rows processed, skip/rollback trends

**Preventive measures**
- Synthetic load test in CI with scaled-down data — catches regressions before prod
- Track data-volume growth rate; alert when projected to exceed SLA
- Quarterly query plan review on reader queries
- Capacity review matching DB resources to growing workload

sections.title: Patterns, Anti-Patterns, and What Good Debugging Looks Like
sections.content:
**When systematic diagnosis helps:**
- Long-standing jobs with grown-organically codebase
- Multi-system pipelines where the bottleneck could be anywhere
- Incidents where the cause isn't an obvious recent change

**When jumping straight to a fix helps:**
- Recent deploy strongly suspected — revert first, diagnose later
- Obvious DB lock-storm visible in metrics — kill blockers first
- Known seasonal volume spike — apply pre-planned scaling

**When scaling without diagnosis hurts:**
- Adding partitioning when the cause is a missing index — 10 workers doing 10× the unnecessary work
- Bumping chunk size when retry storms are the cause — you've made each rollback more expensive
- Adding async processor when the writer is the bottleneck — futures pile up

**Watch for:**
- **Over-tuning chunk size** — 100→500 gives 2-3×; 500→2000 gives 10-30%; diminishing returns
- **Under-recognizing failure-driven slowdown** — retry storms can double run time silently
- **Non-idempotent side effects under retry** — emails fired twice, cards charged twice
- **Reading from replica without lag awareness** — just-written data missing
- **Ignoring the deploy log** — the slowdown often coincides with a release
- **Disabled non-essential constraints never re-enabled** — silent data corruption

**Idempotency is the unsung hero**
- Every parallelism, retry, and skip scheme assumes re-processing is safe
- If the processor sends emails or charges cards, you must use idempotency keys or the outbox pattern
- This concern often drives the architecture more than the parallelism choice

**When to re-architect vs tune**
- At 80% SLA growing 20% YoY — tune now, plan CDC/streaming next year
- At 150% SLA, must run — emergency partitioning + re-architect
- Always slow, now impossible — probably not tuning's fault; rethink the workload

**A good post-incident writeup answers:** - What was the symptom (duration, failure rate)?
- When did it start?
- What changed around then?
- What was the root cause?
- How did we verify the cause (evidence)?
- What's the fix?
- How was it validated?
- What alerts/tests prevent recurrence?
- Was there a longer-term design change discussion?

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Don't scale before diagnosing** — gather StepExecution, DB, host, and volume metrics first.
- **Compare slow vs fast run** — the step that grew most is the bottleneck.
- **Three root-cause categories** — volume growth, throughput regression, failure-driven.
- **Quick wins** — chunk size, JDBC batch alignment, missing index, ANALYZE, off-peak scheduling.
- **Scaling levers** — partitioning, async processor/writer, replica reads, bulk loaders.
- **Idempotency** enables parallelism, retry, and skip safely.
- **`rollback_count` climbing** is a retry-storm signal — find failing records and route to DLQ.
- **Bulk loaders** (`COPY` / `LOAD DATA INFILE`) beat row-by-row inserts for big loads.
- **Observability** — Micrometer Batch metrics + dashboard + alerts on duration and skip rate.
- **Document** root cause and fix; add CI perf tests to catch regressions.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
I'd treat slowdown and failure as potentially separate problems and triage in three phases.

**Phase 1 — gather data (15 minutes):**
- StepExecution history from BATCH_* tables — duration, read/write counts, skip and rollback counts per step
- Actuator metrics — `spring.batch.chunk.write` and `spring.batch.item.process` p50/p99
- DB-side — slow query log, `pg_stat_statements`, lock waits, replication lag
- Host — CPU, GC pauses, disk IO
- Compare a recent 6h run against an older 2h run; the step that grew most is the bottleneck

**Phase 2 — hypothesis testing:**
- Volume growth (40% of cases) — `read_count` larger than last month; throughput unchanged
- Throughput regression (25%) — same volume, slower; check query plans, missing indexes, lock contention
- Failure-driven (15%) — `rollback_count` climbing; retry storms; identify the exception and decide to skip, retry less, or fail fast
- Infrastructure regression (10%) — DB downsized, slower storage, JVM upgrade, network change

**Phase 3 — fix in tiers:**
- Quick wins first — chunk size 100→500→1000→2000, JDBC batch alignment, missing index, ANALYZE, off-peak
- Scaling — partitioning by hash key, async processor/writer for per-item I/O, read from replica, bulk loaders
- Re-architect — CDC/streaming, materialized views, analytical engines

**Patterns to call out:**
- Don't scale before diagnosing — adding partitioning when the cause is a missing index just makes 10 workers do 10× the wasted work
- Over-tuning chunk size has diminishing returns; 100→500 is 2-3×, 500→2000 is 10-30%
- Idempotency is non-negotiable for retries, skip, and partitioning
- Retry storms can silently double run time

**Documentation and prevention:**
- Build a slow-job runbook with exact SQL, actuator endpoints, log commands
- Add alerts on duration thresholds, skip rate, rollback count
- Synthetic load test in CI with scaled-down data
- Track volume growth and alert on projected SLA breach

In an interview I'd emphasize that the first question is always 'how much did the data grow?' — answers the problem in five minutes more often than candidates expect.

followup_questions: How do you detect a retry storm early from metrics alone?
What's your rollback plan when a tuning change goes wrong in production?
When would you recommend moving from Spring Batch to streaming CDC?
How do you test batch performance regressions in CI?

questions.question: A nightly batch job partially completed, then crashed, leaving the target table in an inconsistent state. How do you safely restart and recover without duplicating committed work?
questions.title: Scenario — Restarting a Crashed Batch Job Without Duplicates
questions.direct_answer: First, **stop the bleeding** — confirm no other process is still writing to the target table; mark the abandoned `JobExecution` as `FAILED` so restart can proceed. Then **assess what got committed** — query the BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION row for the failed run and compare `read_count`/`write_count` against the target table to identify which slices completed cleanly. **Restart strategy** depends on idempotency: if writers are **UPSERT-based or use idempotency keys**, a plain restart is safe (committed chunks will be re-read but not duplicated); if writers are **non-idempotent** (`INSERT`-only), you must either delete the partial rows for the failed step or restart with parameters that target only the unprocessed range. Always **document the recovery action** as a post-incident runbook and add idempotency to the writer for the next time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can reason about partial commits, restart semantics, and the operational cost of non-idempotent writers under failure
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Spring Batch restart magically prevents duplicates — it only works correctly if writers are idempotent
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION_CONTEXT inspection, the cleanup-then-restart pattern, and how to retrofit idempotency to a legacy non-idempotent writer

sections.title: Restart Safety Hinges on Writer Idempotency, Not on the Framework
sections.content:
When a batch job crashes mid-run, the target table is in a partial state — some chunks committed, the failing chunk rolled back, and remaining work undone. Restart safety depends on three things working together.

**The three pieces:**
- **Spring Batch restart** — same `JobInstance`, new `JobExecution`; `ExecutionContext` resumes the reader at the last committed checkpoint
- **Writer idempotency** — committed rows that get re-read are written safely (UPSERT, idempotency keys, deduplication)
- **Operational state cleanup** — abandoned `JobExecution` rows in STARTED status block restart until cleaned up

**Without idempotent writers, restart is dangerous:**
- A chunk that committed before crash is on disk
- On restart, the reader resumes at the last committed offset — but if the offset wasn't saved correctly, items may re-read
- Non-idempotent `INSERT` writers create duplicates
- Side effects (emails, API calls) fire again

**The recovery decision tree:**
- Idempotent writer → plain restart is safe; the framework handles it
- Non-idempotent writer with clean slice boundary → delete partial rows, restart
- Non-idempotent writer without clean boundary → manual reconciliation; consider running a one-off cleanup job
- Side effects already fired → assess business impact; may need compensating actions

**The forward-looking lesson** is always to retrofit idempotency to the writer so the next failure is recoverable without manual intervention.

sections.title: Phase 1 — Stop the Bleeding and Assess State
Phase 2 — Choose the Restart Strategy by Writer Idempotency
sections.content:
The restart strategy depends entirely on whether the writer is idempotent.

**Strategy A — Idempotent writer (safest path)**
- UPSERT semantics: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE` (Postgres) or `INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE` (MySQL)
- Idempotency keys: business records carry a unique key; UPSERT on it
- Restart simply re-launches with the same `JobParameters`
- Spring Batch resumes from the last committed chunk
- Re-read items pass through writer's UPSERT — no duplicates

```java
@Bean
public JdbcBatchItemWriter<Order> upsertWriter(DataSource ds) {
    return new JdbcBatchItemWriterBuilder<Order>()
            .dataSource(ds)
            .sql("""
                INSERT INTO orders (id, customer_id, amount, processed_at)
                VALUES (:id, :customerId, :amount, :processedAt)
                ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE
                SET customer_id = EXCLUDED.customer_id,
                    amount = EXCLUDED.amount,
                    processed_at = EXCLUDED.processed_at
                """)
            .beanMapped()
            .build();
}
```

**Strategy B — Non-idempotent writer with clean slice boundary**
- Writer is plain `INSERT` (no UPSERT)
- Job is partitioned and you know which partition failed
- Delete partial rows for the failed partition; restart

```sql
DELETE FROM orders
WHERE batch_run_id = :failedExecutionId
  AND partition_key = 'partitionFour';
```

Then launch with the same parameters — Spring Batch reads the failed partition's StepExecution, resumes via ExecutionContext, processes the partition from the checkpoint.

**Strategy C — Non-idempotent writer without clean boundary**
- Writer is `INSERT`-only and the job is single-step (not partitioned)
- Resume from checkpoint risks duplicates if the checkpoint is imprecise
- Two options:
  - **Delete and re-run** — `DELETE FROM orders WHERE batch_run_id = :failedExecutionId`; relaunch with new parameters; full re-process
  - **Manual reconciliation** — run a one-off step that finds duplicates by business key and deletes them; then continue

**Strategy D — Side effects already fired**
- Emails sent, API calls made, Kafka events published — these are NOT rolled back by chunk failure
- Identify what fired:
  - Outbox table query (if outbox pattern in use)
  - Audit log of external calls
- Decide on compensating action:
  - Send 'correction' notification to recipients of erroneous emails
  - Issue 'cancel' API calls if the downstream system supports it
  - Publish compensating Kafka events
- **The forward-looking fix is to defer side effects to a final step** that runs only after the chunk step completes successfully

**Triggering the restart**

```java
@Component
public class JobRestartTrigger {
    private final JobOperator jobOperator;
    private final JobExplorer jobExplorer;

    public Long restart(String jobName) throws Exception {
        JobInstance lastInstance = jobExplorer.getLastJobInstance(jobName);
        return jobOperator.restart(
            jobExplorer.getLastJobExecution(lastInstance).getId());
    }
}
```

`JobOperator.restart(jobExecutionId)` is the canonical API — it creates a new `JobExecution` for the same `JobInstance` and resumes from the failed step.

sections.title: Phase 3 — Forward-Looking Fixes and Operational Hygiene
Restart Strategy by Writer Idempotency
sections.content:
Pick the strategy that matches the writer's idempotency guarantee.

| Writer Type | Restart Strategy | Manual Cleanup Required |
|---|---|---|
| UPSERT or idempotency-keyed | Plain restart with same `JobParameters` | None — framework handles it |
| Non-idempotent INSERT, partitioned | Delete partial partition rows; restart | Per-partition DELETE |
| Non-idempotent INSERT, single-step | Delete all run rows; relaunch with new params | Full DELETE; full re-process |
| Side effects already fired (emails, API) | Compensating action; restart business logic | Business-impact assessment |

sections.title: When Restart Helps, When It Hurts, and What to Watch
sections.content:
**When restart-from-checkpoint helps:**
- Long-running jobs where partial failure means hours of wasted work
- Idempotent writers that handle re-reads safely
- Partitioned jobs where only failed partitions need to re-run

**When restart hurts:**
- Non-idempotent writers — duplicates without manual cleanup
- Side effects already fired — re-running compounds the problem
- Imprecise reader checkpoints — multi-threaded steps where ExecutionContext is approximate

**When delete-and-rerun helps:**
- Small enough datasets that re-processing is cheaper than reconciliation
- Cases where partial state is hard to identify precisely
- Jobs without natural slice boundaries

**When delete-and-rerun hurts:**
- Very large datasets where re-processing takes hours
- Cases where downstream systems have already consumed the partial output
- Workloads with strict SLAs that can't absorb the re-run window

**Watch for:**
- **Restart on STARTED execution** — `JobExecutionAlreadyRunningException`; abandon first
- **Multi-threaded step + restart** — ExecutionContext may be imprecise; risk of duplicates
- **Side effects already fired** — emails, API calls, Kafka events not rolled back
- **No batch_run_id tagging** — can't identify which rows came from which run
- **Cleanup tasklet runs on the same DB as the job** — may compete for connections during recovery
- **Restart parameter uniqueness** — using `RunIdIncrementer` creates a new JobInstance, NOT a restart

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Restart safety = writer idempotency + framework checkpoint + operational cleanup** — all three required.
- **Abandon stuck `JobExecution`s** before restart — `JobOperator.abandon(id)` or DB update.
- **UPSERT writers are the canonical idempotent pattern** — `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`.
- **Partitioned jobs restart only failed partitions** — major scalability and recovery benefit.
- **Side effects must be deferred** — emails, API calls, Kafka events not rolled back; use outbox or final tasklet.
- **Tag rows with `batch_run_id`** — enables precise cleanup and audit.
- **Test restart in CI** — inject failure mid-job; assert resume + no duplicates.
- **`RunIdIncrementer` creates a new JobInstance** — that's NOT a restart; restart reuses the same JobInstance.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When a batch job crashes mid-run, restart safety hinges on writer idempotency — not on the framework alone.

**Phase 1 — stop the bleeding and assess:**
- Stop the scheduler so nothing else triggers the job
- Confirm no concurrent writers on the target table
- Mark the abandoned `JobExecution` as FAILED with `JobOperator.abandon(id)` so restart can proceed
- Inspect `BATCH_STEP_EXECUTION` to see what got committed — `write_count`, `commit_count`, exception text
- Cross-reference with the target table — query rows by `batch_run_id` if you tagged them

**Phase 2 — pick a restart strategy by writer idempotency:**
- Idempotent writer (UPSERT or idempotency keys) — plain restart with same parameters; framework resumes from checkpoint; no duplicates
- Non-idempotent writer with clean partition boundary — delete partial rows for failed partition; restart
- Non-idempotent writer without boundary — delete all run rows and relaunch with new parameters, OR run a manual reconciliation step
- Side effects already fired (emails, API calls, Kafka) — these are NOT rolled back; assess business impact and issue compensating actions

**Triggering the restart:**
- `JobOperator.restart(failedJobExecutionId)` — canonical API; creates a new JobExecution for the same JobInstance
- Resumes from the failed step using `ExecutionContext` checkpoint

**Phase 3 — forward-looking fixes:**
- Retrofit idempotency to the writer — UPSERT semantics is the most direct fix
- Add a cleanup tasklet that abandons stuck executions automatically
- Move side effects out of the chunk transaction — outbox pattern or final tasklet
- Add observability — Micrometer counter for partial failures, dashboard for STARTED-status executions
- Document the recovery runbook with exact SQL, restart commands, and compensating actions
- Test restart in CI by injecting deliberate mid-job failure

**Common pitfalls:**
- Assuming Spring Batch restart magically prevents duplicates — only true with idempotent writers
- Using `RunIdIncrementer` thinking it restarts — it actually creates a new JobInstance
- Multi-threaded step restart — ExecutionContext may be imprecise
- Side effects fired before crash — emails, API calls, Kafka events not rolled back

In an interview I'd emphasize that the operational answer to 'how do I restart?' is always 'how idempotent is the writer?' — that determines whether the framework can do the work or whether you need manual cleanup.
